items.title: Cold All Night
items.question: I hum without a song, I am cold without a winter, and I keep your dinner safe until morning. What am I?
items.hintText:
I never sleep, and I work hardest in silence.
Open my door and a small light greets you.
Leftovers trust me more than the counter.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The kitchen appliance stays cold around the clock and glows softly when its door opens.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is refrigerator. Continuous cold, a hum, and a little interior light all point to the appliance that preserves food, not an oven or a freezer alone.
items.lessonContent:
Identify an object by the job it performs.
Continuous work often hides in plain sight.
Setting narrows the field quickly.
Test each clue against the candidate.
Share this: describe tonight one household object using only its behaviour.

items.title: Morning Bread Pop
items.question: I wait for bread, then warm it until it launches itself at me. What am I?
items.hintText:
Two or four slots are my only rooms.
A dial decides how dark things get.
Breakfast is my whole career.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The toaster takes slices, browns them, and springs them up when done.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is toaster. The leap of the bread and the darkness dial rule out an oven or a microwave.
items.lessonContent:
Functional clues describe what an object does.
Precise verbs narrow a category fast.
Odd details are often the most identifying.
Match every clue, not just the first.
Share this: name tonight one appliance by its strangest habit.

items.title: Floor Swallower
items.question: I eat crumbs, dust, and stray hair, yet I never get full. What am I?
items.hintText:
I roll across the floor on small wheels.
My mouth is wide and noisy.
When I am done, a bag or a bin sits heavier.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The vacuum consumes debris from floors and stores it in a bag or canister.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is vacuum. Rolling motion, a wide noisy mouth, and collected dirt distinguish it from a broom or a mop.
items.lessonContent:
Cause and function can identify an object.
Notice what a thing takes in and where it goes.
Noise and motion are useful clues.
Reject candidates that match only one hint.
Share this: guess tonight what one machine does from its sound alone.

items.title: Handle Left Alone
items.question: Turn me and water obeys; leave me and it waits patiently. What am I?
items.hintText:
I live at the edge of a basin.
Hot or cold depends on which way you move me.
A drip from me at night is a famous annoyance.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The faucet releases water on demand and is notorious for dripping when worn.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is faucet. Sitting by the basin, controlling temperature, and dripping at night set it apart from a shower head or a pipe.
items.lessonContent:
Objects are defined by the control they exert.
Small fault symptoms can identify a device.
Location narrows possibilities.
Match the setting as well as the action.
Share this: notice tonight one fixture you use without ever naming.

items.title: Daylight Gate
items.question: I hang still, yet I decide whether morning enters your room. What am I?
items.hintText:
I am cloth that folds in pleats.
A rod holds me above a window.
Pull me shut and the world disappears.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The curtain hangs on a rod and controls how much light and view enter a room.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is curtain. Cloth, pleats, a rod, and control of light fit a window covering, not a door or a wall.
items.lessonContent:
Objects can be identified by what they block or allow.
Material and mounting are strong clues.
Consider what an object separates.
Use the whole clue set before deciding.
Share this: think tonight about what one object in your home controls.

items.title: Silent Number Keeper
items.question: I hold a number you rarely see, and I argue with the weather on your behalf. What am I?
items.hintText:
I sit on a wall and watch the temperature.
Turn my dial and a furnace or fan responds.
Your comfort is my only concern.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The thermostat senses temperature and switches heating or cooling to hold a set point.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is thermostat. It reads temperature and commands the system, unlike a thermometer that only reports.
items.lessonContent:
Some devices act on information rather than matter.
Distinguish measuring from controlling.
A set point is a goal an object maintains.
Think of what responds when a device changes.
Share this: find tonight one object that quietly maintains a condition for you.

items.title: Button Without a Body
items.question: I have buttons but no body, and I command a box from across the room. What am I?
items.hintText:
I run on small batteries and point with light you cannot see.
Lose me and the couch becomes a prison.
My buttons change channels and volumes.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The remote control sends invisible signals to operate a television or similar device.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is remote control. Handheld buttons and an invisible beam distinguish it from a phone or a game controller.
items.lessonContent:
An object can act at a distance.
Invisible signals still count as effects.
Form follows the function of controlling another thing.
Consider what a device is pointed at.
Share this: notice tonight how many things you operate without touching.

items.title: Tether of Life
items.question: I am limp and useless alone, but connected, I bring something back from the dead. What am I?
items.hintText:
One end plugs into a wall or a port.
The other end fits a small socket.
Without me a device slowly loses its voice.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The charging cable carries power from a source into a battery-powered device.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is charging cable. Only a power lead links a socket to a device and revives it, unlike earphones or a data drive.
items.lessonContent:
Some objects function only in a connection.
A bridge between two things has a distinct role.
Consider the direction of flow.
Power and information are different loads.
Share this: trace tonight where one cord in your home carries its power.

items.title: Private Whisperer
items.question: I speak into ears no one else can hear, and a wire sometimes keeps me on a leash. What am I?
items.hintText:
Two small speakers sit at my ends.
I turn a shared room into a private one.
Tangle me in a pocket and you will regret it.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! Earphones deliver sound directly to the listener's ears, keeping it private.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is earphones. Paired speakers worn at the ears and the habit of tangling point to personal audio, not a radio or a speaker.
items.lessonContent:
Objects can be defined by their audience.
Private versus shared use is a strong clue.
Small form often signals personal function.
Match every hint before committing.
Share this: notice tonight one object that creates privacy in public.

items.title: Paper Storyteller
items.question: I take silent instructions and cover paper with them. What am I?
items.hintText:
I sit on a desk and tremble as I work.
Ink or powder is my only voice.
Something warm and flat comes out of me.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The printer turns digital instructions into marks on paper.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is printer. Converting data into a warm sheet distinguishes it from a scanner, which works the other way.
items.lessonContent:
Some devices translate between media.
Direction of conversion identifies the machine.
Heat and sound are clues to a working process.
Know what goes in and what comes out.
Share this: identify tonight one device that turns a file into a physical thing.

items.title: Little Metal Bite
items.question: I bite paper and leave two small marks behind. What am I?
items.hintText:
I hold a strip of wire inside my jaw.
Press my top and I clinch a small bracket.
Teachers and clerks keep me within reach.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The stapler drives a metal staple through sheets to bind them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is stapler. Biting sheets and leaving a bent wire bracket is unique to it, unlike a hole punch or a paperclip.
items.lessonContent:
Mechanism plus result identifies a tool.
The material consumed is a strong clue.
A small action can have a lasting effect.
Distinguish joining from puncturing.
Share this: name tonight one tool you know by the mark it leaves.

items.title: Glowing Marker
items.question: I am bright and transparent at once, and I make words shout without changing them. What am I?
items.hintText:
I have a wide tip and a cap that snaps.
My colour is loud but my line is see-through.
Students drag me across important sentences.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The highlighter lays a translucent bright band that makes text stand out.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is highlighter. A broad see-through stroke over existing words is its signature, unlike a pen or a crayon.
items.lessonContent:
Some tools emphasise rather than replace.
Transparency makes a useful visual clue.
Colour can carry a function.
Think of what remains visible underneath.
Share this: notice tonight how you mark what matters in a text.

items.title: Bent Wire Grip
items.question: I am a single wire folded twice, and I hold pages without leaving a wound. What am I?
items.hintText:
I slip over a corner and squeeze gently.
Unbend me and I stop being useful.
Offices pour me out by the boxful.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The paperclip grips sheets by spring tension and can be removed without damage.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is paperclip. Its bent double loop and gentle hold distinguish it from a staple, which pierces the page.
items.lessonContent:
Temporary solutions differ from permanent ones.
Shape can reveal a mechanism.
Reversibility is a design property.
Distinguish holding from fastening.
Share this: find tonight one object you can use and undo cleanly.

items.title: Stretch and Snap
items.question: I am small, dull, and endlessly flexible, and I can snap back from any insult. What am I?
items.hintText:
Stretch me and I store energy.
A bundle of pens and a rolled newspaper both obey me.
I crumble and perish if left in the sun.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The rubber band stretches elastically and returns to shape, holding bundles together.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is rubber band. Elastic springiness and decay in sunlight mark it as rubber, unlike string or tape.
items.lessonContent:
Materials have characteristic behaviours.
Elasticity is a property worth naming.
Environmental weakness can be a clue.
Notice what an object does when released.
Share this: spot tonight one object whose power lives in its stretch.

items.title: Unseen Pull
items.question: I reach across a gap and pull metal toward me without a hand. What am I?
items.hintText:
My power passes through paper and glass.
Two of us can repel as easily as attract.
Doors and notes cling to me.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The magnet exerts an invisible force that attracts iron and some metals across space.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is magnet. Action at a distance through materials is its signature, unlike glue which must touch.
items.lessonContent:
Forces can act without contact.
Invisible influences are still real effects.
Polarity creates attraction and repulsion.
Consider what works through a barrier.
Share this: notice tonight one force you rely on that you cannot see.

items.title: Popping Field
items.question: I am a sheet of tiny pillows, and people squeeze me just for the sound. What am I?
items.hintText:
I protect what is fragile inside a box.
Each of my pockets holds a puff of air.
Nobody can resist pressing just one.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! Bubble wrap cushions fragile items with sealed air pockets that pop under pressure.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is bubble wrap. Rows of air-filled pockets and the irresistible popping distinguish it from foam or paper padding.
items.lessonContent:
Packaging is designed around fragility.
Many small units can cushion a whole.
Sensory appeal can reveal an object's identity.
Think of what protects by absorbing.
Share this: notice tonight one material designed to take a hit for something else.

items.title: Straight and Numbered
items.question: I am long, straight, and covered in small marks that settle arguments about size. What am I?
items.hintText:
My edge is true and my numbers march in order.
Some of me fold or roll away.
Builders and students keep me close.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The ruler provides a straight edge and a marked scale for measuring length.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ruler. A straight edge with numbered units measures length, unlike a tape measure's flexible case or a protractor's arc.
items.lessonContent:
Measurement turns comparison into numbers.
A standard scale lets people agree.
Straightness has uses beyond measuring.
Notice the units an object carries.
Share this: find tonight one thing whose whole job is to compare sizes.

items.title: Fast Thumb Helper
items.question: I hold no thoughts, yet I win arithmetic races against almost everyone. What am I?
items.hintText:
I am small enough for a pocket or a desk.
My face is covered in digits and signs.
Press me and a screen answers instantly.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The calculator performs arithmetic instantly from keyed input and shows the result.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is calculator. Digital keys and an instant display separate it from an abacus, which needs a moving hand and beads.
items.lessonContent:
Tools can outsource a mental task.
Speed is a clue to a dedicated device.
Input and output shape an object's form.
Know what a machine replaces.
Share this: notice tonight one habit you have handed to a machine.

items.title: Ancient Counting Frame
items.question: I count without electricity, using beads that slide on rods. What am I?
items.hintText:
I am a frame with parallel wires.
Each row of beads stands for a place value.
Traders used me centuries before screens.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The abacus is a manual counting frame whose sliding beads represent numbers.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is abacus. Wooden beads on rods and no power source distinguish it from an electronic calculator.
items.lessonContent:
Old tools encode knowledge in their structure.
Place value can be represented physically.
Absence of power is itself a clue.
Think of how a device stores meaning.
Share this: learn tonight one tool people used before your lifetime.

items.title: Falling Sands
items.question: I measure time by losing what I hold, and I must be flipped to start again. What am I?
items.hintText:
I am two glass bulbs joined at the waist.
Sand runs from top to bottom.
I am useless lying on my side.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The hourglass measures a fixed interval by sand draining from one bulb to the other.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is hourglass. Twin glass chambers and falling sand mark it as a timer, unlike a clock face or a candle.
items.lessonContent:
Time can be measured by a changing quantity.
Physical processes can serve as standards.
Orientation can be essential to function.
Notice what must reset a device.
Share this: time tonight one task using something that runs out.

items.title: Mouth Gardener
items.question: I work in a wet, dark place twice a day, and I leave it cleaner than I found it. What am I?
items.hintText:
I am long and thin with a bristled head.
I live near a tube of paste.
My owner replaces me every few months.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The toothbrush scrubs teeth and gums with bristles during a daily routine.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is toothbrush. Bristles, a handle, and a home by the sink identify it, unlike a comb or a razor.
items.lessonContent:
Routines create familiar objects.
Bristles imply scrubbing.
Location and timing narrow the field.
Think of what an object cleans.
Share this: notice tonight one small tool you use on autopilot twice a day.

items.title: Drain Rescuer
items.question: I press and pull where nobody wants to look, and I restore the flow. What am I?
items.hintText:
I have a rubber cup on a stick.
I work by suction and a firm seal.
Plumbers call on me when water refuses to leave.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The plunger uses suction to clear a blocked drain or toilet.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is plunger. A rubber cup on a handle and a suction action distinguish it from a brush or a mop.
items.lessonContent:
Pressure differences can move stubborn things.
Tools are shaped by the problem they solve.
A firm seal enables a force.
Notice what a tool pushes or pulls.
Share this: name tonight one tool whose whole power is suction.

items.title: Wet Floor Dancer
items.question: I glide across a wet floor and leave it cleaner, though I never dance on my own. What am I?
items.hintText:
I am a long stick with soft strands at the bottom.
I am soaked in a bucket before I work.
I follow spills and footprints.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The mop absorbs and scrubs liquid from floors with a long handle and strands.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is mop. A handle with wet absorbent strands sets it apart from a broom, which works dry, or a rag used by hand.
items.lessonContent:
Think of what an object absorbs.
Handle length tells you how it is used.
Dry and wet cleaning are different jobs.
Match the tool to the substance.
Share this: notice tonight which chores call for wet tools and which for dry.

items.title: Thirsty Square
items.question: I drink a great deal, but only so I can give it all back. What am I?
items.hintText:
I am soft, full of holes, and often yellow or green.
Squeeze me and water pours out.
I live near a sink and dislike being left damp.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The sponge soaks up liquid in its porous structure and releases it when squeezed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sponge. A soft porous block that absorbs and wrings out is distinct from a cloth or a brush.
items.lessonContent:
Porosity explains absorbency.
An object can be defined by what it holds temporarily.
Squeezing returns what was taken in.
Notice the texture that enables a function.
Share this: find tonight one object whose usefulness comes from its holes.

items.title: Pocket Sun
items.question: I hold a tiny sun in my hand and point it wherever I choose. What am I?
items.hintText:
I run on batteries and shine a narrow beam.
Twist or click me to switch on.
I am vital when the power fails.
items.correctExplanation: Yes! The flashlight projects a beam from a battery-powered bulb or LED.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is flashlight. A handheld, battery-lit beam separates it from a lamp or a candle.
items.lessonContent:
Portable light changed how people move at night.
A beam is directed, not ambient.
Power source shapes a device's role.
Think of what an object makes possible.
Share this: notice tonight one object that gives you light wherever you go.
